doc.title: Daryl Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 11, 2024

title: Nicki Parrott and substituting for Dave McKenna at the Copley Plaza
summary: Prompted by a Nicki Parrott quote, Sherman tells how she subbed for Dave McKenna in Boston and won over skeptical patrons, and praises McKenna as a song player.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: So I know you know Nicki Parrott.
Oh. They went down under, back to Aussie.

Yes she did. I miss her. She’s played up here on occasion and — I want to read a very brief quote from my interview with Nicki. And this is when she was younger, and she said, “I was so conscious of being taken seriously. There was one instance when I got called for a gig and they said, ‘Is this Nick Parrott?’ I said, ‘Well actually it’s Nicki.’ And the person said, ‘A bass player?’ ‘Yeah, Nicki Parrott.’ Click.” Phone hangs up. Have you ever had that happen to you?

Oh sure. A lot of people — first of all I knew — I was seeing her more often in the days when Arbors had those wonderful jazz parties in Florida, and then of course she moved to New York and we’ve done some gigs together and she was just starting to sing then. And I feel so complimented now because she said, “Oh Daryl, you’re a real singer.” Well look what’s happened. Look what happened to her. Just, well, because of the name, particularly if they don’t — oh, here’s a good story. Here’s a good story: One summer in the ‘80s Dave McKenna first of all was playing at the Copley Plaza which was the best gig. He was playing solo, they gave him a room upstairs, bathtubs were big, he loved it. He was in heaven. However, he wanted to have a summer off to play in the Cape for whatever reason, and I got asked to play. I can’t believe it. Even now I can’t believe it.

And I was there for at least a couple of summers. But okay, first of all, it’s Boston, that was a busy hotel then, and it was Dave’s room and the bar was filled with I could see, I know the type. A lot of them were Madison Avenue types in New York at the bar talking amongst themselves, and I was at the — I guess to the entrance of the room and I go to like the side part of the bar before I’m starting. And I hear the discussion. “So who the hell is this guy Daryl somebody or other who thinks he can play Dave’s piano. What nerve.” And I swear to you it’s true, this is how it happened. And I’m just standing there. So I wait, they’re going on and on and then finally I just go — and I just walk to the piano and I sit down and start playing. And the room is silent. And it took a while. It took a while. They wouldn’t even come near me. But you know what? I managed to win some of them over and when they knew that I adored Dave, that we had so much, you know, family in common and lucky for me one of his staples, because that was what was so wonderful about Dave McKenna, he could play any jazz song and he could play standards and he could play Bobby Short songs or any oddball things. “Sand in My Shoes.”
I pulled out a quote from him, from his interview, that he said, “I’m more of a song player than a jazz player.”

Yes. And I cry when I think about it. He can just play two measures of an introduction, just that, maybe three, and he is already inside the song. And yes, that’s what makes him so extraordinary. And just he didn’t brag about it, it was just who he was, just who he was, all those songs. “Dream Dancing” yeah. So anyway as far as Daryl is concerned, it still happens.
